title: Songs of the road (Psalm 120 [121])
hook: pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem sang these: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains

segments.voice: Yesterday, ner, the small clay lamp. Your line was enough light for the next step. Today, the road itself.

Two hours into a long family car trip, somebody starts a song, everybody knows the words, and the miles go faster. Now take away the car. Families walking for days toward Jerusalem for the great feasts: grandparents, kids, neighbors from the same village. The last stretch is uphill all the way, because Jerusalem sits high in the hills. And as they climbed, they sang. The Psalter kept their road songs, fifteen of them in a row.
screen: `A SONG ON A LONG TRIP.` → `FAMILIES WALKING TO JERUSALEM.` → `UPHILL, SINGING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Fifteen psalms in a row carry the same heading. In Hebrew it's shir ha-ma'alot, a song of the goings up. The Latin Bible made it canticum graduum, a song of the steps, so the Douay-Rheims calls each one a gradual canticle. Gradual here has nothing to do with slowly; it comes from the Latin gradus, a step. Other English Bibles call them the Songs of Ascents. Second, the steps. Nobody knows for certain why they got the name. Some readers think it's the climb up to Jerusalem. An old Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, says the Levites sang on fifteen steps in the Temple, one song for each step. Either way, these are songs for people on the move, going up. Third, today's psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." A pilgrim looks up at the hills, a long climb ahead. Where does help come from? Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the promise: "Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel." On the road you sleep in the open, and someone has to keep watch. The psalm says someone is. Catholics still pray the gradual psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and this one is sometimes prayed for travelers, and at funerals, for the last journey.
screen: `A SONG OF THE STEPS.` · `THE CLIMB, OR FIFTEEN TEMPLE STEPS.` · `HELP FROM THE MAKER OF THE HILLS.` · `SOMEONE KEEPS WATCH.` · then, large: `I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES TO THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Look up at something high, a tree, a rooftop, a hill, the ceiling, the sky through a window, and let your eyes rest there while you name the climb in front of you this week. If you pray, say the line: my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. If you don't, just stay with the looking up, and let your shoulders drop.
Gradual psalms. From the Latin for steps: fifteen songs for going up. Today's word.
Your line: help comes. The pilgrims are nearly at the gates. Day one hundred eighty-four, climbed.

notes: Douay-Rheims 120:1–2 and 120:4 given from memory; confirm.
Gradual psalms are 119–133 in the Vulgate/Douay numbering (120–134 Hebrew); heading 'A gradual canticle' in Douay-Rheims; confirm.
Mishnah tradition of fifteen steps corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents (Middot 2:5, Sukkah 5:4): confirm references.
Use of Psalm 121 for travelers and at funerals: common practice (it appears among psalms for the Office of the Dead and prayers for journeys); confirm.
'Jerusalem sits high in the hills': general geography, stated loosely.
